newsitem.title: VIETNAM: U.N. urges Vietnam to "stay the course" of reform.
newsitem.headline: U.N. urges Vietnam to "stay the course" of reform.

text.p: The United Nations warned Vietnam on Tuesday that unless it implements further economic and social reform, the impressive rates of growth and poverty reduction it has enjoyed in recent years could slow down.

"If economic growth is to continue to translate into improved quality of life for all people. the government will need to widen and deepen its reform process," U.N. Resident Coordinator in Hanoi Roy Morey told a news conference.
"The message is -- stay the course," he said.
Despite a decade-old drive to revamp the Soviet-style economy, more than half the communist country's 75 million people still live below an internationally recognised poverty line.

Fifty-two percent of Vietnam's children are malnourished and millions of its ethnic minorities, who account for 13 percent of the population, suffer from food shortages for about three to four months a year.

In a 187-page report co-sponsored by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund (UNICEF), the Hanoi government was urged to step up measures to eliminate poverty.
"Much more needs to be accomplished...to ensure that the poorest of the poor are not left out of the development process," said Morey, who was presenting the report, "Catching Up".

Since market economy principles and a more open-door foreign policy were cautiously adopted in the late 1980s, the war- battered and internationally isolated economy has come a long way. Annual growth has averaged 8.2 percent over the past five years.
After months of internal debate over the pace and scope of further reform, the Communist Party agreed at a landmark congress five months ago to continue along the same track.

But conservative elements within the party are still pulling the other way, notably by promoting the state sector. Problems of red tape, rampant corruption and a primitive legal system continue to hamstring the economy.
The U.N. report will serve as a guide to donor nations and agencies which are due to hold a World Bank-chaired Consultative Group meeting in Hanoi early next month to decide on aid pledges for 1997.
Donors have become increasingly sympathetic in recent years, bumping up pledges to $2.3 billion last year from $1.8 billion in 1993, when they held their first conference on Vietnam.

"The donor community wants to give a vote of confidence to Vietnam for its reform efforts," Morey said. "The message from this report for the Consultative Group meeting is -- so far, really quite good."

However, he stressed that with an open-door policy, "the door swings in both directions". Hanoi could not simply rely on an inflow of foreign aid, investment, technology and managerial know-how but had to take steps of its own.

These should include trade liberalisation to boost exports, sweeping reforms of the unwieldy state sector, bolstering the non-state sector, improving the legal and banking systems and ensuring greater economic transparency, he said.
